code.title: Image layers are shared; each container gets a writable layer
code.python:
# Image layers are read-only; each container adds its own writable layer.
image = [
    {"/etc/app.conf": "mode=prod", "/bin/app": "v1"},   # base layer
    {"/app/data.txt": "seed"},                          # app layer
]

class Container:
    def __init__(self, image):
        self.image = image      # shared, never modified
        self.upper = {}         # private writable layer

    def read(self, path):
        if path in self.upper:  # newest layer wins
            return self.upper[path]
        for layer in reversed(self.image):
            if path in layer:
                return layer[path]
        return None

    def write(self, path, value):
        self.upper[path] = value  # copy-on-write: image untouched

a, b = Container(image), Container(image)
a.write("/app/data.txt", "changed by A")
print("image layers:", image)
print("A sees:", a.read("/app/data.txt"))
print("B sees:", b.read("/app/data.txt"))
print("A writable layer:", a.upper)
del a                                  # removing a container drops its layer
print("image after delete:", image[1])

followUps:
Under Docker's data directory, by default /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff for that container, on the host.

With the overlay2 driver the image layers are the read-only lowerdir stack, and the container's own changes land in upperdir (the diff folder); the merged view is mounted for the container. docker inspect shows the paths under GraphDriver.Data. Removing the container deletes that folder, so anything written there is lost.

The image ID is the hash of the image's local config JSON; a repo digest is the hash of the manifest as stored in a registry.

They differ because the manifest also lists compressed layer hashes, so one image can have an ID locally and a different digest per registry or per platform (an index digest covers all platforms). Deploy by digest: app@sha256:ab12... is what the registry will return, whereas the ID cannot be pulled. docker images --digests shows both.

Use the shell form, or run a shell yourself, because exec form does not expand variables.

CMD ["echo", "$PORT"] prints the literal text $PORT. Two fixes:

CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec app --port $PORT"]
# or an entrypoint script ending in:  exec "$@"

The exec replaces the shell so the app becomes PID 1 and still receives SIGTERM. Without exec you are back to a shell that swallows signals.

STOPSIGNAL sets which signal docker stop sends first; the default is SIGTERM.

Some programs shut down gracefully on a different signal, for example nginx uses SIGQUIT and some Java setups use SIGINT. Write STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT in the Dockerfile (or --stop-signal at run time). If the process has not exited after the grace period (10 s by default, -t to change) Docker sends SIGKILL, exit code 137.

Without a shell you debug from outside the container, or attach a temporary debug container.

Read docker logs and docker inspect first. Then use docker debug IMAGE if available, or the debug image variant (gcr.io/distroless/base:debug has busybox), or share namespaces: docker run -it --pid=container:app --network=container:app busybox. In Kubernetes, kubectl debug -it POD --image=busybox --target=app adds an ephemeral container. Do not bake a shell into production just for this.

Exit code 125 means the Docker daemon itself failed to run the container, before your command started.

Typical causes are a bad docker run flag, a port already allocated, an invalid mount or an unknown option. The error text is printed by the CLI, not in docker logs. Compare: 126 means the command exists but cannot be executed (permissions), 127 means command not found, and 137 means SIGKILL, often out of memory.

code.title: Layer cache: file order decides what rebuilds
code.python:
# Build cache: a layer's key = parent key + instruction + its inputs.
def build(cache, steps):
    key, misses = "", 0
    for cmd, inp in steps:
        key = key + "/" + cmd + ":" + inp   # parent key is part of the key
        if key in cache:
            state = "HIT "
        else:
            cache.add(key)
            state = "MISS"
            misses += 1
        print("  " + state + " " + cmd + " " + inp)
    return misses

def good(v):  # manifest first, source last
    return [("FROM", "node20"), ("RUN", "apt-get"), ("COPY", "package.json"),
            ("RUN", "npm-ci"), ("COPY", "src-" + v)]

def bad(v):   # everything copied before install
    return [("FROM", "node20"), ("RUN", "apt-get"), ("COPY", "all-" + v),
            ("RUN", "npm-ci")]

for name, layout in (("good order", good), ("bad order", bad)):
    cache = set()
    print(name + ": first build")
    build(cache, layout("v1"))
    print(name + ": after editing source")
    n = build(cache, layout("v2"))
    print("rebuilt layers:", n)

followUps:
Because the layer is cached by the text of the command, so an old package index can be reused long after the repository moved on.

If RUN apt-get update sits alone, later RUN apt-get install foo runs against a weeks-old index, and the package version it lists may have been removed from the mirror, giving a 404. The fix is one instruction: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y foo && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. Then the index and the install always cache together.

An ARG is part of the cache key of every instruction after it, so changing it rebuilds everything below.

If you put ARG GIT_SHA at the top and pass a new commit hash on every build, the key of all later layers changes and nothing is reused, so a 20-minute dependency install runs every time. Declare such args as late as possible, just before the step that uses them, and keep stable ones (like a base version) early.

Because the secret is already in the image and in anyone's copy of it, so deleting the image does not undo the leak.

Assume anyone who could pull it (or any CI log, cache or mirror) has the value. Revoke and replace the credential first, then check access logs for misuse, and only then delete the image and purge caches. If you delete first, you lose the evidence you need and the key stays valid. Rotating takes minutes; deleting every copy is impossible.

The convention lets you give a variable's value as a file path, so the secret is read from a mounted file instead of the environment.

For example POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_pass: the entrypoint script reads that file and exports POSTGRES_PASSWORD itself. This keeps the value out of docker inspect and /proc/<pid>/environ of other tools. Compose or Swarm mounts the file under /run/secrets. It only works if the image's entrypoint supports it, as the official Postgres and MySQL images do.

Anyone who can talk to that socket can control the Docker daemon, which runs as root on the host, so it is effectively root on the machine.

From inside the container they can start a new privileged container with the host's / mounted:

docker run -v /:/host --privileged alpine chroot /host sh

So a compromised app with the socket owns the host. If a tool needs it (CI, Traefik), use a socket proxy that allows only read-only endpoints, or use rootless Docker or Podman.

Docker keeps a trimmed list of 14 capabilities, such as CHOWN, NET_BIND_SERVICE, KILL, SETUID, SETGID and DAC_OVERRIDE, and drops dangerous ones like SYS_ADMIN and NET_ADMIN.

Most apps need none of them. The safe pattern is to drop all and add back only what is required:

docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE app

A non-root app on port 8080 needs no capability at all.

Use the host's gateway name, because inside the container localhost is the container itself.

On Docker Desktop use host.docker.internal. On Linux add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway (compose: extra_hosts), or use the bridge gateway IP, often 172.17.0.1. The host service must listen on that interface, not only on 127.0.0.1. Or use --network host on Linux, at the cost of isolation.

In rootless mode networking runs in user space (pasta or slirp4netns), so it is slower and has a few limits.

Throughput is lower than a kernel bridge, the container sees the real client IP only with pasta or special settings, and ports below 1024 cannot be published unless net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start is lowered. There is no direct container-to-container IP routing across users. In exchange, a breakout gets only your user's rights, not root.

Run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and archives it to a bind-mounted host folder.

docker run --rm -v data:/src:ro -v $PWD:/out alpine \
  tar czf /out/data.tgz -C /src .

Restore by reversing it with tar xzf into an empty volume. For databases a file copy of a running server may be inconsistent, so prefer pg_dump or stop the container first. Test restores regularly; an untested backup is a hope.

Because every file access has to cross a virtual machine boundary between macOS and the Linux VM that runs Docker.

A bind mount of a folder with 50,000 files (such as node_modules) makes each stat and read a round trip, so builds can be many times slower. Fixes: use a named volume for heavy folders like node_modules, enable VirtioFS in Docker Desktop, or sync code with docker compose watch. On Linux there is no VM, so bind mounts are native speed.

The migration service fails, exits non-zero, and every service that depends on it with service_completed_successfully never starts.

docker compose up reports the dependency failed and stops. Read the migration's logs, fix it, and rerun; the dependent services start only after it exits 0. That is a feature: the app should not run against a half-migrated schema. Make migrations idempotent so a rerun is safe.

Kubernetes has no start-up ordering between pods, so each app must tolerate missing dependencies and rely on probes and init containers.

Use an init container for one-time waiting or migration (the main container starts only after it succeeds), a readiness probe so traffic reaches only ready pods, and a startup probe for slow starts. The app itself retries connections with backoff, because a dependency can restart at any time. Failing pods are restarted with CrashLoopBackOff delays.

code.title: Wait for a dependency with exponential backoff
code.python:
# Waiting for a dependency: poll its health with exponential backoff.
class Database:
    def __init__(self, ready_after):
        self.ready_after = ready_after   # becomes healthy after N checks
        self.checks = 0

    def healthy(self):
        self.checks += 1
        return self.checks >= self.ready_after

def wait_healthy(service, max_tries=6, base=0.5, cap=4.0):
    delay = base
    for attempt in range(1, max_tries + 1):
        if service.healthy():
            print("attempt", attempt, "-> healthy, starting app")
            return True
        print("attempt", attempt, "-> not ready, would wait", delay, "s")
        delay = min(delay * 2, cap)      # 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 4 ...
    print("gave up: exit non-zero so the orchestrator restarts us")
    return False

print("slow database (ready on check 4)")
wait_healthy(Database(4))
print("dead database (never ready)")
wait_healthy(Database(99))

followUps:
npm does not forward signals or reap children, so the app often never gets SIGTERM and Docker kills it after 10 seconds.

npm start as PID 1 launches sh -c node server.js, so signals hit npm, not node, and npm may not pass them on. Result: slow stops, exit 137, dropped requests. Run CMD ["node", "server.js"] directly, and add --init or tini if it spawns children.

Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits for the grace period (30 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL.

The pod is also removed from Service endpoints at the same time, but that is asynchronous, so requests may still arrive. A common pattern is a preStop sleep of a few seconds, then graceful shutdown in the app within terminationGracePeriodSeconds. If shutdown needs 60 s, raise the setting; the app must handle SIGTERM as PID 1.

You see exec format error when starting, or a warning such as image platform (linux/amd64) does not match the detected host platform (linux/arm64).

It happens when an amd64-only image runs on an ARM machine without emulation, or the reverse. Docker may run it slowly under QEMU if emulation is set up, otherwise the binary fails to execute. Fix by building a multi-arch image or passing --platform explicitly.

BUILDPLATFORM is the machine doing the build; TARGETPLATFORM is the platform the final image will run on.

On an amd64 laptop building for arm64, BUILDPLATFORM is linux/amd64 and TARGETPLATFORM is linux/arm64. Use FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang so the compiler runs natively, then cross-compile with GOARCH=$TARGETARCH. This avoids slow QEMU emulation for compile steps.

Run it with an ephemeral debug container that shares the target's namespaces, since the image itself has no shell.

With Kubernetes use kubectl debug -it POD --image=busybox --target=app; with Docker use --pid=container:NAME --network=container:NAME on a busybox container. You can then see its processes, ports and /proc/1/root files. Alternatively build a :debug variant of the image. Keep production images shell-free.

Logs can be empty when the process died before writing anything, or wrote to a file instead of stdout/stderr.

Common causes: the app logs to /var/log/app.log inside the container (Docker only captures stdout and stderr), output was buffered and lost on a SIGKILL (Python needs -u or PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1), the container was recreated so the old logs went with it, or the log driver is not json-file. Check docker inspect for the exit code too.

Rootless containers trade some performance and features for a much smaller blast radius if an attacker escapes.

Costs: slower user-space networking, no ports under 1024 by default, limits on cgroup resource controls, limited storage drivers (fuse-overlayfs) and some images that assume real root fail to chown files. Benefit: container root maps to an unprivileged host user, so a breakout cannot touch other users' data or system files. Good default for CI and shared hosts.

On Linux, Docker Engine runs natively on the host kernel; Docker Desktop runs the engine inside a hidden Linux VM.

So with Desktop, bind mounts cross a VM boundary (slower), the host's real IP and ports are reached through forwarding, and resources (CPU, memory) are capped by the VM settings. Desktop also bundles extras (Kubernetes, a GUI, extensions) and has licensing terms for larger companies. Engine is leaner for servers.

Because a digest covers the bytes of every layer, and builds usually are not bit-for-bit reproducible.

Timestamps in files, an unpinned apt-get install or npm install fetching newer versions, file order in tarballs, and build metadata all change the bytes, so the hash changes. Even the same source can give two digests. For reproducibility pin base images by digest and dependencies by lockfile, and set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH.

Promote by retagging or copying the exact same digest, never by rebuilding.

After staging tests pass, run docker buildx imagetools create -t registry/app:prod registry/app@sha256:ab12... (or crane copy), and deploy production with that digest. Because nothing is rebuilt, production runs exactly the bytes you tested. Add an approval gate, and record digest, commit and scan result for the audit trail.
